questions.q: What is lineage documentation, as defined in this lesson?
options: The recorded, shareable version of the dependency graph, instead of something that lives only in one person's memory
A list of every employee in the data team
A single diagram with no supporting text
The source code of the ETL pipeline itself
questions.explain: Lineage documentation makes the downstream and upstream walks from Chapter 3 possible by recording the dependency graph in a shareable form.

questions.q: What three things does this lesson say good lineage documentation should capture for every dependency?
options: Nodes, edges, and ownership
File size, row count, and creation date
Server IP address, port number, and protocol
Only the names of the two datasets involved
questions.explain: Nodes (the datasets/fields/reports), edges (the dependency and its transformation), and ownership (who's responsible for each side) are the three things worth recording.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does documentation missing ownership undermine a change impact assessment?
options: Because it tells you what is affected by a change but not who to contact about it
Because ownership information is required by law in every industry
Because a dataset without a listed owner cannot be queried
Because ownership is the only thing a lineage tool can ever capture
questions.explain: Knowing a consumer exists without knowing who owns it leaves a dead end exactly where Lesson 15's sign-off and communication step needs a real contact.

questions.q: According to the lesson's comparison, what is the main weakness of a wiki page as a location for lineage documentation?
options: It goes stale fast because nobody reliably updates it on every pipeline change
It cannot contain any text describing a dataset
It is the only option that can auto-generate from code
It requires expensive dedicated tooling to set up
questions.explain: A wiki page is easy to write and flexible, but unlike a dedicated lineage tool, it doesn't automatically stay in sync with the actual pipeline.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say lineage documentation needs both the structural graph and the transformation logic behind each edge?
options: Because an arrow alone ('this feeds that') is only half the picture, per Lesson 13's point about business rules hiding in transformations
Because structural graphs are no longer used in modern tooling
Because transformation logic is only relevant to root cause analysis, never documentation
Because nodes and edges are the same thing and only need to be recorded once
questions.explain: Capturing only the connection without the logic behind it leaves documentation incomplete in a way that becomes obvious the first time someone actually relies on it.
